Simulation studies of the paper

Source: vignettes/simulation.Rmd
simulation.Rmd

This vignette reproduces the simulation studies of Section 5.2 of Hu and Yi (2026) with BiSCaL. It describes the designs, computes the true values of the effects, analyzes one simulated data set, and summarizes a full run of the studies (100 replicates of each design).

library(BiSCaL)

Designs

Each simulated data set has n = 5000 subjects followed at a baseline visit and K = 20 follow-up visits. There is one standard normal covariate X, and a treatment assigned with probability 0.5. The binary responses follow models (12)–(14) of the paper. All coefficients equal 0.5 except the treatment coefficients (\beta_{1,3,1}, \beta_{2,3,1}):

  • case 1: (5, 0.1), the treatment mainly affects the first response;
  • case 2: (0, 0), no treatment effect;
  • case 3: (0.1, 5), the treatment mainly affects the second response.
biscal_coefs(case = 1)$beta1
#>               1
#> (Intercept) 0.5
#> y1[k-1]=1   0.5
#> y2[k-1]=1   0.5
#> trt         5.0
#> x           0.5

simulate_biscal() generates complete data (Section 5.2.2), or data with censoring and intermittent missingness (missing = TRUE, Section 5.2.3). In the latter, subject i is followed up to visit C_i \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(20, \sigma(1.5 + x_i)). At each follow-up visit, the two responses are missing with probabilities \sigma(x_i) and \sigma(x_i - 0.5).

d <- simulate_biscal(n = 5000, K = 20, case = 3, missing = TRUE, seed = 1)
head(d)
#>   id visit trt          x y1 y2
#> 1  1     0   0 -0.6264538  0  0
#> 2  1     1   0 -0.6264538  0  0
#> 3  1     2   0 -0.6264538  0  1
#> 4  1     3   0 -0.6264538  1  1
#> 5  1     4   0 -0.6264538  1  1
#> 6  1     5   0 -0.6264538  1  1
mean(attr(d, "censoring"))                     # mean censoring time
#> [1] 15.5218
fu <- d[d$visit > 0, ]
c(mean(tapply(is.na(fu$y1), fu$id, mean)),     # mean missingness rates
  mean(tapply(is.na(fu$y2), fu$id, mean)))
#> [1] 0.5018990 0.3963568

True values

The target is DEASTE_K = E|STE_{1,K}(X)| - E|STE_{2,K}(X)| at K = 20, the expectation being over X \sim N(0, 1). biscal_truth() computes it by numerical integration:

truth <- t(sapply(1:3, function(case) biscal_truth(K = 20, case = case)))
rownames(truth) <- paste("case", 1:3)
signif(truth, 4)
#>             ESTE1     ESTE2      ETTE    EASTE1   EASTE2    DEASTE
#> case 1 -0.0099080 -0.003365 -0.006636 0.0099080 0.003393  0.006515
#> case 2  0.0000000  0.000000  0.000000 0.0000000 0.000000  0.000000
#> case 3 -0.0001733 -0.093830 -0.047000 0.0001755 0.093830 -0.093660

These are the values T in Tables 5 and 7 of the paper. Case 1 gives 6.515 \times 10^{-3}, against 6.535 \times 10^{-3} in the paper, whose value was computed by Monte Carlo integration.

One replicate

Each replicate fits the models, then estimates DEASTE_{20} as an average over 10,000 draws from the covariate distribution. It tests H_0: DEASTE_{20} \ge 0 against H_1: DEASTE_{20} < 0:

fit <- biscal(cbind(y1, y2) ~ x, data = d, id = "id", time = "visit", treatment = "trt")
set.seed(2)
draws <- data.frame(x = rnorm(10000))
res <- easte(fit, newdata = draws, K = 20)
res$test
#>    K   estimate  std.error statistic      p.value
#> 1 20 -0.1299243 0.01597084 -8.135095 2.058078e-16

The estimate from a single data set carries sampling error. The repeated replicates below show the behavior of the estimator.

The full study repeats this 100 times for each design. The code is in data-raw/simulation-study.R in the package sources. It uses parallel::mclapply() and takes about 2 seconds per replicate and core.

one_rep <- function(i, case, missing) {
  seed <- 100000 * missing + 1000 * case + i
  d <- simulate_biscal(n = 5000, K = 20, case = case, missing = missing, seed = seed)
  fit <- biscal(cbind(y1, y2) ~ x, data = d, id = "id", time = "visit",
                treatment = "trt")
  set.seed(seed + 500000)
  e <- easte(fit, newdata = data.frame(x = rnorm(10000)), K = 20)
  list(coef = coef(fit), se = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit))), deaste = e$test$estimate,
       se_deaste = e$test$std.error, p = e$test$p.value)
}
reps <- parallel::mclapply(1:100, one_rep, case = 1, missing = FALSE, mc.cores = 4)

Results of the full study

The results of the full run are stored in the package:

sim <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "simulation-study.rds", package = "BiSCaL"))
sim$settings
#> $n
#> [1] 5000
#> 
#> $K
#> [1] 20
#> 
#> $n_draws
#> [1] 10000
#> 
#> $R
#> [1] 100

Separable effects (Tables 5 and 7)

For each design, the table gives the true value (T) and the average estimate (AE). It also gives the average standard error (ASE), the average p-value of the test (AP) and the coverage (CP, %) of the 95% confidence interval:

summ_deaste <- function(r) {
  covered <- abs(r$deaste - r$true_deaste) <= qnorm(0.975) * r$se_deaste
  c(T = r$true_deaste, AE = mean(r$deaste), ASE = mean(r$se_deaste),
    AP = mean(r$p), CP = 100 * mean(covered))
}
tab <- t(sapply(sim$results, summ_deaste))
rownames(tab) <- sprintf("case %d, %s", sapply(sim$results, `[[`, "case"),
                         ifelse(sapply(sim$results, `[[`, "missing"),
                                "missingness and censoring", "complete data"))
signif(tab, 3)
#>                                          T        AE      ASE       AP CP
#> case 1, complete data              0.00652  0.006390 0.001290 1.00e+00 93
#> case 2, complete data              0.00000 -0.000392 0.000541 2.72e-01 96
#> case 3, complete data             -0.09370 -0.094500 0.006240 1.39e-47 98
#> case 1, missingness and censoring  0.00652  0.006100 0.002890 9.42e-01 96
#> case 2, missingness and censoring  0.00000 -0.000782 0.001230 3.02e-01 96
#> case 3, missingness and censoring -0.09370 -0.093700 0.013300 1.15e-10 91

As in the paper, the sign of the estimated DEASTE_{20} matches the design:

  • case 1: positive, and the test does not reject H_0;
  • case 2: close to zero;
  • case 3: negative, and H_0 is rejected.

The coverage of the confidence intervals is close to the nominal 95%.

Model parameters (Tables 4 and 6)

The same summaries for the coefficients of the regression models; the labels follow the notation of the paper:

labels <- c("beta[1,0,1]", "beta[1,1,1]", "beta[1,2,1]", "beta[1,3,1]", "beta[1,4,1]",
            "beta[2,0,1]", "beta[2,1,1]", "beta[2,2,1]", "beta[2,3,1]", "beta[2,4,1]",
            "gamma[1,0,1]", "gamma[1,2,1]", "gamma[2,0,1]", "gamma[2,1,1]", "gamma[2,2,1]")
summ_coef <- function(r) {
  covered <- abs(sweep(r$coef, 2, r$true_coef)) <= qnorm(0.975) * r$se
  data.frame(T = r$true_coef, AE = colMeans(r$coef), ASE = colMeans(r$se),
             CP = 100 * colMeans(covered), row.names = labels)
}
for (r in sim$results) {
  cat(sprintf("\nCase %d, %s\n", r$case,
              if (r$missing) "missingness and censoring" else "complete data"))
  print(signif(summ_coef(r), 3))
}

The estimates are close to the true values and the coverage is close to 95%. This reproduces the conclusions of Tables 4 and 6.

The numbers differ from the published tables because the replicates use different random numbers. For the design with missingness and censoring, the data generation is also implemented differently: here, no visit after the censoring time C_i is recorded. With 100 replicates, the Monte Carlo standard error of a coverage near 95% is about 2.2 percentage points.

Reference

Hu, P. and Yi, G. Y. (2026). Inference about separable causal effects with longitudinal bivariate ordinal responses with missingness and censoring. Statistics in Medicine, 45, e70320. https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.70320
